why_this_matters: The history is more than a purchase date. Naming Yovawan and Aswaw, then tracing English grants of inheritance, trade and government, shows how colonial authority was layered over an existing Native homeland. history_title: Native parties and the English machinery of ownership
history_content:
An island with Native names and relationships

Gardiners Island lies in the bay between Long Island's two eastern forks, north of East Hampton. The 1639 agreement calls it Manchonat; later English grants also record Manchonack and rename it the Isle of Wight. These names place a Native homeland beneath the better-known English family name. The island's history begins before the documents that colonial owners later used to establish their title. The Papers and Biography of Lion Gardiner: 1639 agreement Records of the Town of East-Hampton: James Farrett grant

Yovawan, Aswaw and Lion Gardiner

The agreement dated May 3, 1639 names Yovawan, sachem of Pommanocc, and Aswaw, described in the reproduced text as his wife, as the Native parties. It names Lion Gardiner, commander of Saybrook Fort on the Connecticut River, as the recipient. The transcription records ten coats of trading cloth as payment and uses English conveyancing language extending the grant to Gardiner's heirs and assigns. The Papers and Biography of Lion Gardiner: 1639 agreement

This record matters because familiar retellings replace the named parties with Wyandanch or repeat a story about a dog, gun and rum. The published document identifies different parties and payment. Naming Aswaw also keeps a Native woman who appears in the agreement from disappearing in a story told only through male colonists. The surviving English wording does not, by itself, tell us everything the Native parties understood or expected. The Papers and Biography of Lion Gardiner: 1639 agreement

An English agent claimed authority over an earlier agreement

James Farrett, acting for the Earl of Stirling, acknowledged that Gardiner had obtained possession from the island's Native inhabitants before Farrett arrived. Nevertheless, his grant required Gardiner to hold title through the Earl, whose authority it traced to the English king. The document therefore reveals two different sources of claimed authority: an agreement with Native people and a royal claim asserted over their homeland. Records of the Town of East-Hampton: James Farrett grant

Farrett's terms allowed Gardiner and his successors to build, plant and dispose of the island, and to establish church and civil government. They also reserved broader trade with Native people to the Earl, while allowing Gardiner to obtain food for the plantation, and required an annual payment. This was a claim over government and commerce as well as land. The document bears the date March 10, 1639 under the calendar then used in England; that written date must not be casually placed before the May agreement without considering the old March beginning of the legal year. Records of the Town of East-Hampton: James Farrett grant

From a family estate to a colonial manor

On October 5, 1665, English governor Richard Nicolls confirmed the island to David Gardiner, Lion's son and heir. The grant covered land and resources including woods, marshes, waters, fishing and hunting. It gave the island privileges comparable to a town, made it accountable to the governor rather than another town for the specified matters, and required an annual payment of five pounds. Deeds of Gardiners Island: Nicolls and Dongan patents

On September 11, 1686, governor Thomas Dongan granted David a further patent establishing the Lordship and Manor of Gardiners Island. Its powers included holding manor courts and collecting specified rents and fines. The patent also recited governor Francis Lovelace's 1670 reduction of the earlier annual payment to one lamb. Successive English governors were reinforcing inherited ownership and local authority, rather than recording a new agreement with Native signers each time. Deeds of Gardiners Island: Nicolls and Dongan patents

A patent is not the end of Native history

Colonial documents describe what their issuers claimed the power to grant. They cannot establish that Native people disappeared or that every earlier relationship to the island ended. The distinction is especially important here: an agreement naming two Native parties became part of a title history increasingly narrated through an English family, royal authority and inherited governmental privileges.

Montauk people continue cultural and community work today. The Montauk Tribe of Indians describes language revitalization, cultural education and connections among relatives living in many places. That living work offers a different starting point from the idea that Native history ended with a seventeenth-century deed. It is one community's account, not a claim that one organization speaks for every descendant or a new assertion about ownership of this particular island. Our Story and Language Revitalization
